title: Jump Game — Greedy Reachability, One Pass at a Time
summary: Greedy reachability tracking for Jump Game I and II, and why maximizing reach at each step is always safe — even though it looks like it's throwing away information.

slides.markdown:
Each array element tells you the maximum jump length from that position. Jump Game I asks: can you reach the last index? Jump Game II asks: what's the minimum number of jumps to get there?

Both are solved with the same core idea — track the **furthest index reachable so far** as you scan once, left to right, and never look back. It's a clean example of a greedy strategy whose safety isn't immediately obvious (why is throwing away all the specific jump choices and keeping only "the furthest point" not losing information?) until you see the exchange-argument-style reasoning behind it.

Scan the array once, keeping a running variable `furthest` = the largest index reachable using any position visited so far. At each index `i`, if `i > furthest`, that index is unreachable — the scan can never get there, so nothing after it matters either. Otherwise, update `furthest = max(furthest, i + nums[i])`.

The entire state needed is that one number. Not which position produced it, not the sequence of jumps that got there — just the furthest boundary itself. That collapsing of a whole set of possible paths into a single number is the crux of why this is a greedy algorithm and not a DP one: it assumes the specific path doesn't matter, only the frontier does.

Picture the array as a line, with a marker showing the current `furthest` boundary. As the scan visits each index up to that boundary, the boundary itself may push further right; the scan continues until either the boundary reaches (or passes) the last index, or the scan's own position outruns the boundary.

<<< Image: a horizontal array of 8 cells with jump values written in each; show a shaded region from index 0 to a boundary marker at index 5 labelled "furthest reachable", with the boundary marker shown moving rightward to index 7 as the scan processes index 3 (which has a large jump value) >>>

The frontier only ever moves forward — it's a monotonically non-decreasing quantity, which is exactly the property the next few slides build on.

slides.subTitle: One-pass feasibility
Greedy level-by-level counting
slides.markdown:
```python
def min_jumps(nums):
    jumps, current_end, farthest = 0, 0, 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
        if i == current_end:
            jumps += 1
            current_end = farthest
    return jumps
```

Think of this as a breadth-first search collapsed into a single pass: `current_end` marks the boundary of everything reachable with the jumps counted so far (one "level"), and `farthest` tracks the best boundary the *next* level could reach. Every time the scan reaches `current_end`, that level is exhausted, a jump is committed, and the boundary advances to `farthest`.

slides.sectionTitle: Greedy pass vs. DP over positions
slides.markdown:
| | Greedy (both versions) | DP over positions |
|---|---|---|
| State kept | One or two running integers | dp[i] = min jumps to reach i, for every i |
| Complexity | O(n) time, O(1) space | O(n²) time in the naive version (for each i, scan all reachable j) |
| What it discards | The exact path/jump sequence | Nothing — every position's best answer is explicitly stored |

A DP formulation of Jump Game II — `dp[i] = 1 + min(dp[j] for all j that can reach i)` — is correct but strictly worse here, because the greedy's collapsing of state loses no information that actually mattered to the answer. This is a good example of "DP still works, but greedy is strictly better once you've verified it's safe" — not every problem gives you that choice.

slides.sectionTitle: Maximizing reach vs. taking the longest jump
slides.markdown:
A tempting but wrong simplification: "at each step, take the single longest jump available." That's not what the algorithm does, and confusing the two produces a broken implementation.

The actual rule maximizes the **running frontier** across *all* positions visited within reach, not the jump length chosen *at* the current position. A position with a small jump value can still be worth visiting if it's on the path to unlocking a position with a much larger jump value further along — "always take the longest single jump" would skip past exactly those smaller-but-strategically-placed positions. The frontier-tracking version implicitly considers every reachable position's jump value, not just the current one's.

slides.sectionTitle: Why maximizing reach is always safe
slides.markdown:
The exchange-argument-style justification: reachability is **monotone** — if you can reach index `k`, you can also reach every index between your start and `k` that lies on some valid path, and having a *larger* furthest-reach value never closes off any option that a *smaller* one would have kept open. A bigger frontier is a strict superset of possibilities compared to a smaller one.

So "maximize the frontier at every step" can never be the wrong local choice — any alternative choice that produces a smaller frontier is dominated, in the sense that everything the smaller frontier could do, the larger one can also do, plus more. That domination argument is the jump-game-specific version of the same swap-and-show-no-harm logic from `exchange-argument`.

Both greedy versions are O(n) time and O(1) space — a single pass, a constant number of tracked variables. The naive DP alternative for Jump Game II is O(n²): for each position, scanning backward (or forward) over every position that could reach it.

Calling out this gap explicitly — "the greedy version is O(n); a DP formulation would be O(n²) and add nothing correctness-wise here" — is worth doing proactively in an interview. It signals you know DP would still be *correct*, just strictly worse, which is a more precise statement than simply not mentioning DP at all.

A single-element array (`[0]`) is trivially reachable — you're already at the last index, and this should return `True`/`0` jumps without the loop needing to run meaningfully. A `0` at the very first position, with more than one element, should immediately fail Jump Game I (`i > furthest` triggers at `i = 1` since `furthest` never moved past 0). A `0` in the *middle* of the array is only a problem if the frontier hasn't already jumped past it — code that assumes any `0` anywhere is fatal is wrong.

These aren't exotic cases; they're exactly the ones a careless implementation gets wrong first, and they're fast to check by hand before declaring the solution done — directly the discipline `live-testing-discipline`, later in this area, generalizes into a habit.

"Track a running boundary of what's reachable, and never let a locally smaller choice replace a locally larger one" reappears well beyond this specific problem — it's the same shape behind sliding-window right-boundary tracking and behind some graph reachability arguments. Whenever a problem's state can be collapsed to "the furthest/best boundary seen so far" without losing information about what's still achievable, that collapse is usually safe, and it's worth actively checking for on any new interval- or position-based greedy problem you meet.
